title: Dynamics and triggers of misinformation on vaccines
screen_reason: Six years (2016-2021) of Italian vaccine-related social media content from a quasi-census of 682 Italian news sources (161 classified questionable, 521 reliable by NewsGuard, Facta, Pagella Politica, bufale.net and butac.it), collected across Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and YouTube. Table 3 gives both a content share and an engagement share of questionable-source material with explicit denominators: 44,547/353,530 contents (12.6%) and 10,898,774/95,230,911 interactions (11.4%). The authors themselves read the content share as prevalence of misinformation ('misinformation making up a relatively small but not insignificant (12.6%) part of all the news content supplied during the period 2016-2021'). Source-level classification against a reliability list, so CONTENT (share of items that exist) plus SHARING (share of engagement).

estimates.measure_type: % of vaccine-related social media content published by Italian news sources that came from questionable (misinformation-spreading) sources
estimates.value_raw: 44,547/353,530 (12.6%) overall; sub-periods reported separately: pre-pandemic 7,567/23,860 (31.7%), pandemic 36,980/329,670 (11.2%)
estimates.denominator: 353,530 vaccine-related contents published on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and YouTube by 682 Italian news sources (96 of the 121 major newspapers, 462 online-only outlets, 89 TV channels, 35 radio stations) between 2016 and 2021
estimates.definition: The content was published by a source classified questionable, i.e. one 'whose reputation is regularly spreading misinformation', on the merged lists of bufale.net, butac.it, facta.news, NewsGuard and Pagella Politica; content was captured by matching an exhaustive vaccine keyword list from the Italian Medicines Agency
estimates.misinfo_def: "their binary classification of news sources into either questionable (indicating a reputation for regularly disseminating misinformation) or reliable (indicating the tendency to adhere to high journalistic standards)"
estimates.source_quote: Although we find misinformation making up a relatively small but not insignificant (12.6%) part of all the news content supplied during the period 2016–2021, information dynamics shifts over time, with the percentage of misinformation nearly tripling (31.7%) when focusing on the period before the Covid-19 outbreak.
estimates.page_loc: Table 3 'Breakdown of the dataset', p. 5; restated in the Conclusions, p. 17
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Binary source-reliability classification imported from independent third-party fact-checking and rating organisations (bufale.net, butac.it, facta.news, newsguardtech.com, pagellapolitica.it); the authors merged their lists and used their factualness classification unchanged. No item-level veracity check was performed, and no reliability statistic applies to the source labels (the 0.88 accuracies reported in the paper belong to the separate stance and topic classifiers, which are not used for the misinformation label).
estimates.moderator_quote: This quasi-census approach applied to both questionable and reliable news sources enabled us to virtually capture the entirety of vaccine-related information provided to Italians in recent years (NewsGuard alone claims to monitor domains covering about 95% of online engagement with news sites). Specifically, we collected all vaccine-related content published by these 682 sources on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and YouTube between 2016 and 2021 ... we searched for content whose textual parts (message, image text, or any other description) matched an exhaustive list of vaccine-related keywords ... The complete list of keywords was retrieved from the website of the Italian Medicines Agency.
estimates.notes: TIME SERIES COLLAPSED to the overall 2016-2021 figure (12.6%), which is the paper's own headline; the two sub-period values are recorded in value_raw because they differ by a factor of three (pre-pandemic 31.7%, pandemic 11.2%) and a reviewer analysing by year should use them rather than the overall figure. year=2018 is the calendar midpoint of the window; note that 93.3% of the content volume falls in the pandemic sub-period (2020-2021), so a volume-weighted year would be much later - flagged for the adjudicator. IMPORTANT SCOPE CAVEAT: the denominator is the output of NEWS SOURCES' social media accounts, not everything users see on these platforms - ordinary users', politicians' and influencers' posts are outside the frame entirely, so 12.6% is the misinformation share of institutional news supply on vaccines, not of the vaccine content circulating in Italy. sampling_frame=full_census reflects the authors' quasi-census of Italian information providers (96/121 newspapers, 462 online outlets reaching ~96% of the Italian internet audience, 89 TV, 35 radio); items within those sources were selected by an exhaustive vaccine keyword list, so an adjudicator could defensibly code keyword_topical instead. breadth is blank per the instructions because the classification is a source-level reliability list, not an item-level veracity judgement.

estimates.measure_type: % of all user interactions with vaccine-related content from Italian news sources that went to questionable-source content
estimates.denominator: 95,230,911 user interactions (the algebraic sum of all actions/reactions - likes, comments, shares etc.) with vaccine-related content from the 682 Italian news sources across the four platforms, 2016-2021
estimates.definition: The interaction was performed on content published by a source classified questionable on the merged fact-checker reliability lists
estimates.misinfo_def: "questionable (indicating a reputation for regularly disseminating misinformation) or reliable (indicating the tendency to adhere to high journalistic standards)"
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same source-reliability lists as the content row (bufale.net, butac.it, facta.news, NewsGuard, Pagella Politica); interactions counted from CrowdTangle for Facebook/Instagram and from the official Twitter and YouTube APIs.
estimates.moderator_quote: Data are divided by source set and period analyzed ... and concern the number of sources, contents, and corresponding user interactions, understood as the algebraic sum of all possible actions/reactions performed on the four platforms analyzed.
estimates.notes: Coded SHARING (sharing_subtype content_share) because the denominator is engagement - likes, comments, shares and other reactions summed - which the instructions route to SHARING rather than EXPOSURE; it is NOT a view or impression count, so it must not be read as an exposure/diet share. unit=exposure is the closest available code for an interaction-denominated figure (there is no 'interaction' unit); the underlying events are engagement actions, not items or people. Time series collapsed to the overall figure; sub-periods in value_raw (33.6% pre-pandemic vs 10.1% pandemic). Because engagement is unnormalised here, this row does not contradict the paper's separate finding that PER-CONTENT engagement normalised by followers is about 6 times higher for questionable sources overall (11 times pre-pandemic): questionable sources have far fewer followers and post far less, so they take a small share of total interactions while over-performing per post. Same scope caveat as the content row: news-source accounts only.

missed_or_uncertain: (a) Platform-specific figures are described only approximately in the text and live in supplementary figures I cannot see: 'approximately half of the vaccine-related content on the platform [Facebook] before the Covid-19 outbreak was indeed generated by questionable sources' and 'the fraction of vaccine-related content from questionable sources stabilized at 10%' during the pandemic. 'Approximately half' is not a number under R8, and the 10% is superseded by the exact 11.2% in Table 3; no platform-level row is therefore extractable, though S2 Fig would presumably support Facebook/Instagram/Twitter/YouTube rows. (b) Stance distributions are NOT veracity measures and were not extracted: anti-vax content 'was clearly dominant throughout the pre-pandemic period ... and drops from 65% to 40%' within questionable sources, while reliable sources' anti-vax share 'exceeds 10% during Covid-19 outbreak' and their neutral share exceeds 65%. Stance is orthogonal to truth in this design (a reliable source can publish anti-vax content, and questionable-source content can be neutral or pro-vax), so treating 65% as a misinformation share would be wrong; if an adjudicator wanted them they would be within_misinfo_content rows for the questionable-source figures. Note also that these values are read off Fig 3 rather than tabulated. (c) Engagement RATIOS (median out-engage factor ~6x overall, ~11x pre-pandemic, ~40x for anti-vax content; medians 26.2 pre-pandemic vs 8.2 pandemic for Q) are ratios, not shares - no denominator, no row. (d) Transfer-entropy, cross-correlation and log-linear regression results are causal/associational. (e) Source counts (161/682 = 23.6% of sources questionable; all but one questionable source is an online-only outlet) are a share of SOURCES, not of content or exposure; potentially usable as a source-level content moderator but not a prevalence estimate, so not extracted. (f) The reach figures used to argue representativeness (newspapers reaching ~60% of Italian adults, online outlets ~96% of the internet audience, TV ~54%, radio ~77%; platform penetration YouTube 85.3%, Facebook 80.4%, Instagram 67%, Twitter 32.8%) are external audience statistics cited from GfK, ComScore, Auditel, RadioTER and GWI - barred by R8. (g) The stance/topic classifier accuracies (0.88 on evaluation; inter-annotator agreement 0.87) apply to the stance and topic models, not to the misinformation label, which is purely source-list based.

rob.design: Observational platform-data study, no human subjects. Source frame: merged reliability lists from five independent Italian fact-checking/rating organisations, yielding 682 sources (161 questionable, 521 reliable) described by the authors as a quasi-census of Italian information providers - 96 of 121 major newspapers, 462 online-only outlets, 89 TV channels, 35 radio stations; all but one questionable source is an online-only outlet. Content: every vaccine-related post by those sources' Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and YouTube accounts, 1 Jan 2016 - 31 Dec 2021, retrieved by matching an exhaustive vaccine keyword list taken from the Italian Medicines Agency (general terms plus vaccine brand names). Collection tools: CrowdTangle (Facebook, Instagram) and the official Twitter (academic access) and YouTube APIs. N = 353,530 contents and 95,230,911 interactions. Misinformation is defined at SOURCE level only - no item was checked for factual accuracy - so the estimate inherits whatever error the third-party lists carry and cannot separate true from false items within a questionable source (or vice versa). Analysis: 30-day moving averages, cross-correlation, Effective Transfer Entropy with bootstrap significance, a follower-normalised 'out-engage factor', and two fine-tuned neural classifiers for stance and topic (accuracy 0.88 on held-out evaluation; inter-annotator agreement 0.87 on the same sets; ~20% double-annotated overlap). Data availability: content IDs and models posted at osf.io/nsmk3.
rob.item6_quote: we identify opinion leaders by consolidating lists from independent third-party organizations (e.g., NewsGuard, Facta, Pagella Politica) and by utilizing their binary classification of news sources into either questionable (indicating a reputation for regularly disseminating misinformation) or reliable (indicating the tendency to adhere to high journalistic standards).
rob.item10_quote: Although we find misinformation making up a relatively small but not insignificant (12.6%) part of all the news content supplied during the period 2016-2021, information dynamics shifts over time, with the percentage of misinformation nearly tripling (31.7%) when focusing on the period before the Covid-19 outbreak.
